entries.title: Art of play in the age of AI
entries.summary: Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here's what we can learn through that process as developers. The post Art of play in the age of AI appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here’s what we can learn through that process as developers.

As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.

In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!

For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.

The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.

Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!! #GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5

— Connie Xu (@conniecodes)October 28, 2026

you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge! repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY

— Rishab Kumar (@rishabincloud)October 27, 2026

Coding needs room for play

According to the Octoverse report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.

With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!

AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.

As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.

You don’t need a big idea to start

What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!

At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.

Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.

AI with oversight

AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.

In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.

Be kind, keep maintainers in mind

It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a lot to the maintenance burden.

Efforts need to be made by all of us, like the one shared here, to help ease burdens for maintainers.

As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”

Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:

  • Read the contribution guidelines
  • Check existing issues
  • Understand what the project needs

Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.

Now it’s your turn

We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does. Give it a go on our virtual badge, and try tinkering on it yourself.

Then get your hands on your own badge. We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code 

FREESHIPBLOG26
for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

entries.title: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
entries.summary: Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill. The post How to choose the next safe step in application modernization appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill.

A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary.

I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable.

This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system.

Build evidence before choosing a target

The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting.

Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory:

  • Manifests, lockfiles, entry points, and deployable components
  • Verified commands for installing, building, testing, packaging, and running
  • Runtime pins in containers, CI workflows, deployment files, and developer tooling
  • External contracts such as APIs, database behavior, file formats, and user workflows
  • End-of-life frameworks and dependencies, with evidence that the application still uses them

Record uncertainty while you work. I use three simple labels: documented, inferred, and unverified. If two files disagree about the Java version, resolve the contradiction. If you can’t determine whether a CI check blocks merges, say so. Record the unknown rather than treating a guess as a finding.

That inventory gives you something concrete to review with the people who own the application before you propose changes.

Choose the least disruptive treatment that works

Once you understand the application, make the decision per component. A single system can contain code that should stay, dependencies that should be swapped, and one subsystem that genuinely needs a rewrite.

First, check whether a capability is still needed. Remove it only after verifying that it is unused or superseded and confirming that decision with its owner. Removal is a separate decision, and it’s not necessarily the most disruptive one.

For a capability you still need, start with the option that changes the least:

  1. Keep it. Supported code that still fits the job doesn’t need a modernization story.
  2. Upgrade it. Move to a supported major version and fix the breaking changes.
  3. Swap it. Replace an abandoned dependency while preserving the existing design.
  4. Wrap it. Stabilize a useful interface and replace the internals in increments.
  5. Rewrite it. Use this when no responsible upgrade path exists or the architecture cannot meet the requirement.

This is a decision order, not a universal ranking of effort or risk. Ask what evidence justifies choosing a more disruptive option. “The code is old” is not enough. A known vulnerability with no patched release for the pinned version, a dependency that fails on the required runtime, or a measured reliability target the current design cannot meet can justify escalation.

Decide what proof is possible

The next question is whether the component can run well enough to produce evidence, even if the legacy CI pipeline is not green.

Run a time-boxed feasibility check. Try to install dependencies, build on an available toolchain, start the component, and execute at least one meaningful test. Stop when the time box expires. The result sends you down one of two paths.

Capture behavior, then upgrade. Use this path when the old application can still run at an acceptable cost. Record its externally visible behavior, fix the test harness where practical, and use those checks to verify the upgrade.

Build a small modern slice first. Use this path when the old component cannot run until you have already changed it. Move the thinnest useful workflow to supported technology, prove it, and expand from there. Requiring a complete legacy test suite in this situation is circular. Restoring the test suite is part of the modernization.

I use the following safety levels, adapted from the 

doc-and-modernize
skill, to describe the strongest regression protection available:

LevelStrongest honest protection
L0No usable regression net; treat the old code and available documentation as the specification.
L1Small reversible changes, old and new paths in parallel, smoke checks, and domain review.
L2Captured inputs and outputs, snapshots, or other behavioral comparisons.
L3Automated checks cover part of the system, with the remaining gaps named.
L4An automated CI gate combines lint, unit, behavioral, and end-to-end checks for the agreed scope.

State what you can prove and what risk remains. Even an L4 gate cannot establish that every possible behavior is correct. APIs, database effects, files, rendered output, and business workflows often make durable comparison points because those behaviors can survive a framework or language change.

PiggyMetrics: capture behavior, then upgrade

PiggyMetrics was the clearest example of an application that looked worse than it was. The project used Java 8, Spring Boot 2.0.3, Spring Cloud Finchley, Zuul, Hystrix, and the old 

spring-security-oauth2
library.

It would have been easy to call the application unworkable and start drawing a new architecture. The feasibility check told a different story.

The recorded feasibility results show these two probes against the legacy checkout with JDK 8:

CommandRecorded resultWhat it established
mvn -pl config -am compile
Exit code 0The selected config module and required reactor dependencies compiled.
mvn -pl account-service -am test
14 tests ran: five passed and nine erroredSome service logic passed; embedded MongoDB initialization blocked the other tests.

These are historical results, not commands expected to reproduce those failures on the modernized checkout. The nine errors traced through 

Failed to load ApplicationContext
to an embedded MongoDB download returning HTTP 403. The pinned binary also targeted i386, which would not run on the Apple Silicon host.

The probes did not establish that the whole application ran or that its integration behavior was correct. They did give me a narrower next step: replace the test dependency and rerun the affected tests before changing the production stack.

That result saved me from making a very tidy, very expensive mistake. I had already started thinking about which parts of the architecture I might replace. One broken test dependency did not justify redesigning the application, and five passing tests established behavior I could check for unintended changes during modernization.

The modernization plan turned that evidence into a capture-then-upgrade sequence:

  1. Replace the embedded database dependency with Testcontainers and establish a green baseline on the existing stack.
  2. Put that baseline in GitHub Actions before changing the production runtime.
  3. Move from Java 8 to Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.3.
  4. Replace obsolete components behind their existing interfaces: Zuul with Spring Cloud Gateway, Hystrix with Resilience4j, and the retired OAuth stack with Spring Authorization Server and JSON Web Token (JWT) resource servers.
  5. Carry the baseline forward and add contract checks around the parts whose behavior changed.

The first acceptance gate was a passing baseline on the old stack, not merely the successful installation of a replacement dependency. Running checks in CI and enforcing them as merge requirements were also separate steps in the plan.

The result summary records the Java and Spring upgrades while retaining the microservice decomposition that the application exists to demonstrate. Eureka and Cloud Config stayed; the two monitoring modules used by the retired Hystrix and Turbine stack were removed. The in-scope build went from nine modules to seven.

Those versions describe the experiment, not a recommendation to select the same versions today. Choose targets against your current support requirements. The useful lesson is how the repository evidence narrowed the change.

The method changes with the system

The same process produced different answers on two smaller applications. Their pinned reports describe these choices:

ApplicationWhat stayedWhat changedStrategy
BrowserQuestCanvas renderer, pathfinding, world model, protocol, and game-loop modelNode 0.4.7 to Node 22, two obsolete WebSocket stacks to 
ws
, plus tests and GitHub Actions		Upgrade and swap
DOOMRenderer, 35 Hz simulation model, and WAD game-data formatX11 video and OSS audio replaced with SDL2; platform code adapted for modern 64-bit systemsPreserve the core and replace the platform

The comparison needs one important qualification: DOOM’s checks froze outputs from the modernized engine itself. They protected against later regressions; they did not independently prove parity with a period-correct legacy binary. Naming that limit is part of choosing an honest safety level.

Scaling the method without pretending the product is finished

I then applied the method to ADempiere, a large Java suite covering ERP, customer relationship management, manufacturing, supply chain, accounting, and point of sale.

The scale changed the controls, but not the method. The work established a reproducible build, moved the runtime to JDK 21, preserved SOAP web-service contracts while replacing XFire with CXF and Jakarta, captured legacy web behavior, and introduced a modern web path for selected users. The first modern business partner write was compared with a result frozen from the legacy application.

The fixed measurement report covers 30 merged modernization pull requests and 102,587.72 reconstructed Copilot credits through the first accepted portable demo. The credit total is not a dollar cost. More important, the report says exactly what the result was not: it was not a claim that every ADempiere screen or production deployment had been modernized.

I stopped because the proof-of-concept question had been answered. The result demonstrated a build on the selected runtime, old and new paths running together, and a real business write checked against the legacy result. Completing the rest would have required a product funding decision, not another technical proof. Stopping at that boundary was part of the method.

Turn the method into an agent skill

After repeating this work, I didn’t want the evidence checklist and decision rules to live only in my notes. I encoded them in the public 

doc-and-modernize
agent skill.

Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when a task is relevant. A project skill can live with one repository:

.github/skills/doc-and-modernize/
├── SKILL.md
├── references/
└── scripts/

Only 

SKILL.md
is required; the resource folders shown here are optional. The file needs YAML frontmatter with a 
name
and a 
description
explaining what the skill does and when to use it, followed by the instructions. The creation guide includes the full format.

Paraphrased from the commit-pinned skill source, its decision fork is:

  • If the old component can run at an acceptable cost, capture its behavior before upgrading.
  • If it cannot run without changes, build and verify a small modern slice first, then expand it.

The full skill adds the feasibility check, testability milestone, safety levels, phase gates, and evidence requirements.

The useful distinction is procedure versus policy. A shared skill can require repository evidence, bounded experiments, explicit safety levels, and runnable exit criteria. Your organization still needs to supply the parts only it knows:

  • Approved runtimes, frameworks, and hosting services
  • Application criticality and acceptable residual risk
  • Security, compliance, and change-control requirements
  • Which legacy or production results may be used as the expected answer
  • Who can approve the architecture and declare a production change complete

The skill should make those decisions visible. It shouldn’t make them for you.

Start with one bounded application

Choose an application with an identified owner, known business value, and one workflow you can observe. Run the documentation workflow first. Review the architecture, commands, runtime surfaces, and unknowns with the people who own the system.

Then approve one experiment, not a portfolio rewrite.

Inspect the skill and its supporting files before adding it to a project. GitHub CLI’s 

gh skill
commands are in public preview; check the current installation guidance when you’re ready to use them.

entries.title: These are the gifts developers will actually want
entries.summary: The developer you're shopping for hasn’t shared their holiday wish list with you yet? Check out these gifts, plus our Black Friday discount all week long. The post These are the gifts developers will actually want appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
The developer you’re shopping for hasn’t shared their holiday wish list with you yet? Check out these gifts, plus our Black Friday discount all week long.

Some people tell you exactly what they want for the holidays, but some people just don’t. The gifts, the decor, the food, for all of it, you have to guess at what they might like. You trawl thousands of gift guide lists titled “the definitive gift guide for 2026,” but none of the guides are quite right for that special person. That is, until this one came along.

As long as that person in your life is a developer.

We won’t say it’s the definitive guide for the developer in your life (or for yourself, we won’t judge), but we have brought together a few of our favorite pieces from the GitHub Shop for you to pick from.

Get building

At GitHub Universe this year we brought our brand new GitHub x Omnitype Bauer Lite Keyboard Kit to the Makerspace for our attendees to build. To say it was popular is an understatement. If you like building keyboards, you’ll want the details. Each GitHub-exclusive Bauer Lite kit arrives in a randomly selected color combination and includes a hot-swap PCB with RGB underglow, Omnitype Hawk linear switches, dye-sublimated PBT keycaps, and the essential hardware and tools for a hands-on custom build. And if you’re new to building keyboards then you can follow along with our step-by-step guide.

If you like building of a different variety, perhaps our new GitHub jigsaw puzzle will be calling you. Grab yourself a hot beverage, settle in, and start building. Speaking of which…

Get cozy

If the preference is to work on the sofa in ultimate comfort, then this is the gift guide for you. Drape a cozy blanket over you, put on some warm socks, and while your agent is busy at work you can slip on the sleep mask and have a little mid-afternoon nap.

Get decorating

If the desk of you or your loved one is looking a bit dull, brighten it up with a colorful desk mat, selection of mugs and tumblers, and two buddies to help with all your coding decisions. The Copilot Amazeball sits on your desk until you have a burning question. Should you ship on a Friday? Give the Amazeball a shake, turn it over, and get your answer. Your other tiny teammate, the Mona Octobobble, will simply nod along to all your best ideas. Of which, we’re certain, there are many.

Get traveling

If your January resolution is to become a digital nomad then there are gifts here for you, too, especially if you have all the ideas but no gear. From tech organizers to work totes to awesome skateboards, we’ll get you where you need to go in style.

Super fans unite

Super fans, check out some of our most popular items from the shop, like our classic invertocat hoodie. Plus get your hands on the matching version for your drink.

Cold outside? Then dress up your outfit with our Mona Varsity jacket. Too warm for that? Then you’ll love our Cabana shirt and shorts co-ord.

Something for the next generation

Whether it’s for a brand-new baby or the tweenager just getting into coding, we have something for all ages. Start them off with the Invertocat onesie and move on into the matching Mona bestie bottle and Mona plush.

Shipping fees? 404 Not Found.

We have a special Black Friday deal for you: Use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026 and ensure your gifts arrive by December 22 by checking out our holiday shipping deadlines. Happy shopping!
